# Retrospective {#sec-retrospective} **You will learn:** - what the rank sweep asks, what it changes and what it holds fixed; - what the adapter of @sec-training can and cannot say about the rank it needs; - how many trainable parameters an adapter of each rank adds; - what is written down before the results of the sweep are seen. The book fine-tuned one model, with one adapter, and a few choices were made without testing the alternatives. This chapter runs one experiment on one of them: a **rank sweep**, the same fine-tuning run at five values of the LoRA rank (@sec-lora), compared on the same validation turns. Afterwards it goes through the other things one could try, and says for each what the earlier chapters already show. ## The experiment The sweep trains four new adapters, with ranks 4, 8, 32 and 64, and sets them beside the rank-16 adapter of @sec-training. The rank is the only thing that changes (with `alpha`, which moves with it so that the scaling stays the same). The data, the learning rate, the number of epochs, the batch size and the seed are those of @sec-training. The sweep asks three things: 1. Does a smaller rank do as well as 16? 2. Does a larger rank do better? 3. Does an adapter with more directions use them? The first two are answered by the accuracy of each adapter on the validation split, in both history modes (@sec-evaluating), and by its paired difference from the rank-16 adapter. The third is answered by the same analysis of the adapter's update that @sec-training made for rank 16. The training loss of each run is the check that the runs differ only in capacity, and not in how they trained. The rest of the chapter sets the sweep up. The next sections say why the rank is the thing to vary and what the rank-16 adapter already tells us, then define the runs and the size of each adapter, and then write down what we expect and how we will read the results, before any of them is seen. ## Why the rank ::: {#1650c488 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from peft import LoraConfig default_rank = LoraConfig().r assert default_rank != 16 ``` ::: The adapter of @sec-training has rank $r = 16$: each adapted matrix is changed by the product of two thin matrices with 16 directions between them. The rank is the capacity of the update. A task that needs the model to change a lot needs a high rank; one that asks for a small, regular change, such as writing programs in a fixed format, may need very little. We fixed 16 before looking at the task, and nothing in the book has tested it. It is not even the default of the PEFT library, which is 8. Full fine-tuning, where every direction of every matrix may change, is not run: the highest rank of the sweep is the nearest it gets. ## What the first adapter says @sec-training looked at the update that the rank-16 adapter made, one matrix at a time, and found that it was small compared with the weights and that it was concentrated in a few directions. ::: {#c19183e7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from convfinqa.artifacts import get stats = get("adapter_analysis_main_0").json("stats.json") sq = np.array([m["singular_values"] for m in stats["matrices"]]) ** 2 share = sq / sq.sum(1, keepdims=True) cumulative = share.cumsum(1).mean(0) assert stats["r"] == 16 assert share[:, 0].mean() > 0.4 and cumulative[7] > 0.85 ``` ::: The largest direction holds on average 56% of the squared norm of an update, and the largest eight hold 93%. That suggests that a rank below 16 might do. It cannot say more than that. An update made with 16 directions is cut off at 16: if the task could use 64, the rank-16 adapter would show a spread that runs to the last direction, and would not show the directions it did not have. The sweep is the way to find out, and the same analysis of a larger adapter says whether it uses the extra directions. ## The runs The ranks are 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64, with 16 in the middle. The rank-16 run is the adapter that every earlier chapter used (`main`). Each of the others is the same run with the rank changed and `alpha` set to twice the rank, so that the scaling $\alpha / r$ that multiplies the update stays at 2 (@sec-lora). They are defined in `configs/train.json` as `rank4`, `rank8`, `rank32` and `rank64`, and each gives the artifacts of @sec-training and @sec-evaluating with its name in place of `main`: `lora_rank64_0` is the adapter, `tuned_val_rank64_0_pred` its answers on the validation split. The seed is 0 for all of them. The number of parameters of an adapter grows in proportion to the rank. For each adapted matrix of shape $d_\text{out} \times d_\text{in}$ the adapter has $r (d_\text{in} + d_\text{out})$ parameters, and the model adapts every linear layer of each of its blocks. ::: {#97d60861 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from transformers import AutoConfig MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507" cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(MODEL) d, heads, kv, hd = ( cfg.hidden_size, cfg.num_attention_heads, cfg.num_key_value_heads, cfg.head_dim, ) # (input size, output size) of the seven adapted matrices of a block SHAPES = { "q_proj": (d, heads * hd), "k_proj": (d, kv * hd), "v_proj": (d, kv * hd), "o_proj": (heads * hd, d), "gate_proj": (d, cfg.intermediate_size), "up_proj": (d, cfg.intermediate_size), "down_proj": (cfg.intermediate_size, d), } per_rank = cfg.num_hidden_layers * sum(i + o for i, o in SHAPES.values()) # the adapter that was trained has the size the formula gives from safetensors import safe_open with safe_open( get("lora_main_0").path / "adapter" / "adapter_model.safetensors", "pt" ) as f: trained = sum( np.prod(f.get_slice(k).get_shape()) for k in f.keys() ) assert trained == 16 * per_rank RANKS = [4, 8, 16, 32, 64] pd.DataFrame({ "rank": RANKS, "alpha": [2 * r for r in RANKS], "trainable parameters": [f"{r * per_rank:,}" for r in RANKS], }).set_index("rank") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
alpha trainable parameters
rank
4 8 8,257,536
8 16 16,515,072
16 32 33,030,144
32 64 66,060,288
64 128 132,120,576
``` ::: ::: The adapter of rank 16 has 33\,030\,144 parameters, which is what the adapter file of `main` holds; each step in the table doubles it, and at rank 64 it has 132 million. ## What is decided before the results One seed per rank is what the budget allows, and that limits what the results can say. The comparison of each run with `main` is a paired difference on the same validation turns (@sec-evaluating). When its interval excludes zero, that run differs from `main` on this split. It does not say the rank is the cause: two runs of the same rank with different seeds also differ, by an amount the sweep does not measure. So a small difference, in either direction, will be reported as not shown, and the sweep is read as a curve: whether the accuracy rises, falls or is flat as the rank changes, not whether any one point is better. The prediction, written before any of these runs: the accuracy is flat from rank 4 to rank 64, with differences that the paired intervals cannot tell from zero. The reasons are that the update at rank 16 is already concentrated in few directions (see "What the first adapter says" above) and that the format of the task is simple. The prediction would fail if the accuracy rose with the rank beyond 16, or fell sharply at the low end (at rank 4 or 8, because the capacity is too small). Rank 64 is four times the default, and the evidence above gives no reason to expect the task to use more. The sweep stops there unless the accuracy is still rising at rank 64, that is, unless rank 64 differs from `main` by a paired interval that excludes zero. In that case ranks 128 and 256 are the next runs, and this chapter will say so. ## Other things one could try {#sec-other-things} The sweep is the one new experiment of this chapter. The other ideas that came up while writing the book are not run, for one of two reasons: the results we already have say that they would not help, or they cost more than the project can show a gain for. The first kind is checked below against the validation results; the second is described, with the reason. ### Not needed: what the results already say ::: {#28707cf2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY import json from convfinqa.stats import bootstrap_accuracy, paired_difference main_pred = get("scores_tuned_val_main_0_pred") main_scores = list(main_pred.jsonl("scores.jsonl")) main_sum = main_pred.json("summary.json") n_val = main_sum["n"] n_invalid = round(main_sum["invalid_rate"] * n_val) n_bad_reference = main_sum["by_kind"]["bad_reference"] # DSL adapter: the numbers it writes, checked against the page (@sec-evaluating-errors) dsl_checks = [ c for c in get("checks_tuned_val_main_0_pred").jsonl("checks.jsonl") if c["runs"] ] dsl_off_page = sum(not c["lit_grounded"] for c in dsl_checks) assert dsl_off_page == 0 assert n_invalid == n_bad_reference == 1 # Python adapter against the DSL adapter (@sec-python-numbers) py_scores = list( get("scores_python_tuned_val_0_pred").jsonl("scores.jsonl") ) py_lead = paired_difference(py_scores, main_scores) assert not py_lead["excludes_zero"] pts = lambda x: f"{100 * x:+.1f}" ``` ::: Three ideas would add a constraint or a variant that the results show to be unnecessary. - **A grammar that allows only numbers from the page.** 0 of the 1\,124 programs of the adapter that run contain a number that is not on the page (@sec-evaluating-errors), so such a grammar would have nothing to forbid. It is the untuned model that writes numbers that are not on the page (@sec-python-numbers). - **A grammar for the `#k` references to earlier steps.** Of the 1\,125 validation turns of the fine-tuned model, 1 is invalid, and it is a reference to a step that does not exist (@sec-constrained-results). A grammar for references could fix at most that turn. - **A Python variant where variables persist across turns,** like a notebook. The Python adapter is \-0\.4 points from the DSL adapter on the validation turns, with a paired interval of \-2\.3 to \+1\.5 (predicted history), so a second Python variant would be measured against a tie. A fourth idea, more training data written by hand or generated, was planned as a chapter of its own and dropped: the chapter used no model, built one example, and could check only its form, so it did not show how such data would be used by the rest of the book. ### Not tried, and why ::: {#9d1939c8 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY vote = list(get("extra_val_main_0_vote_full").jsonl("predictions.jsonl")) group = vote[0]["generations"] unanimous = sum(v["agreement"] == 1 for v in vote) / len(vote) half_width = bootstrap_accuracy(main_scores) half_width = (half_width["high"] - half_width["low"]) / 2 assert unanimous > 0.8 assert half_width > 0.02 ``` ::: - **A stronger model**, untuned or fine-tuned. An untuned stronger model says little about this project, which asks what fine-tuning a small model on the language of the task gains. A fine-tuned larger one is the same experiment at another size, and a project of its own, with its own cost. - **Page images in place of text,** with a vision-language model, and LoRA on its language layers only. The data gives each page as extracted text and a table, and the reports they come from are not part of it; we did not find where to get them. There is nothing to give such a model. - **Reinforcement learning with the executor as the reward.** The execution of a program already gives a reward that needs no judge: 1 if the answer matches, 0 if not. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [@shao2024deepseekmath] samples a group of programs per prompt, scores each, and moves the model towards the ones that score above the average of their group. @liu2025finr1 trained a 7B model this way, starting from a model that had been fine-tuned on examples, and report on ConvFinQA a score of 81.0 for the model before and 85.0 after, on their own sample of questions and prompts, so the numbers are not comparable with ours. Three things argue against running it here, and the first two can be read from the book. First, the signal. The samples of a group that agree on the answer get the same reward, and a group with a single reward has no program that scores above the others. In the self-consistency run of @sec-evaluating, 5 samples per turn agreed on the answer for 92% of the validation turns. A group of eight, which is what TRL uses by default, has more room to disagree, but most of the turns would still give little. Second, the size of a gain. The accuracy of the fine-tuned model on this split has an interval of about ±3\.5 points, so a gain of one or two points is small beside it. A paired comparison is tighter than that, but one seed adds a variation that is not measured (see "What is decided before the results" above). Third, the cost: each prompt needs a full-length sequence for each member of the group, generated during training. The idea is left for a project with more data, more seeds and more budget. - **Training on the model's own predicted history,** which would remove the gap between training and use that @sec-evaluating measures, and **fine-tuning on reasoning traces,** which needs a teacher model to write them. The first needs generation inside the training loop, like the reinforcement learning above, and the second needs a model that we do not have.
